note.question: How does personalizing a marketplace's product ranking change the prices learned by competing pricing algorithms and the welfare of consumers who search sequentially?
note.overview: Competing sellers delegate repeated price choices to independent Q-learning agents. Their rewards depend on a platform's ranking regime and consumers' optimal sequential search, and the learned policies are compared with Bertrand-Nash and monopoly benchmarks.

coverage.note: The existing independently audited model map was decomposed into Mini-style components and linked back to the page-preserving source extraction.

models.name: Repeated multiagent pricing with personalized or unpersonalized search rankings
models.summary: Competing sellers delegate repeated price choices to independent Q-learning agents. Their rewards depend on a platform's ranking regime and consumers' optimal sequential search, and the learned policies are compared with Bertrand-Nash and monopoly benchmarks.
objects: Short-lived consumers making sequential search and purchase decisions
inputs: Sellers observe the previous period's price vector
Consumers observe prices and qualities, know match-value distributions, and learn product-specific match values through search
Personalized ranking uses predicted consumer-specific utility; unpersonalized ranking uses aggregate expected utility
Pricing agents do not communicate, share Q-tables, or condition on consumer identities
decisions: Each seller's agent chooses a price from a discretized action set
Each consumer decides whether to stop or search the next product
Each agent updates its state-action value and subsequent pricing policy
assumptions: Each seller supplies one vertically differentiated product at a fixed marginal cost and has no capacity constraint
A new unit mass of consumers enters each period; match values are independent Type-I extreme-value draws and become known only after search
The first search is free, later searches are costly, consumers can take an outside option, and they use an optimal stopping rule
The main computational environment is an asymmetric duopoly with a one-period price vector as the Markov state and discretized price actions
The platform's ranking regime is fixed rather than strategically reoptimized during the repeated pricing interaction

components.label: Learned Q-learning rest-point outcomes with Bertrand-Nash benchmarks
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Learned Q-learning rest-point outcomes with Bertrand-Nash benchmarks. Section 3.3 says the price points to which competing Q-learning algorithms converge can be viewed as a rest-point equilibrium. The article compares those computational rest points with one-shot Bertrand-Nash and monopoly prices and probes them through one-shot deviations and learned punishment paths; it does not prove a general analytical equilibrium theorem for the learning process.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: A personalized or unpersonalized ranking rule is fixed exogenously for an experimental condition. In every period, sellers' Q-learning agents simultaneously choose prices based on the preceding price state; the platform mechanically applies the fixed rule; a new consumer cohort searches sequentially and buys; sellers observe profit rewards and update Q-values before the next period. Ranking changes demand elasticity and therefore both the immediate benefit of undercutting and the learned punishment needed to sustain high prices. Consumers are short-lived, while pricing agents condition current prices on the previous joint price state.
